sites.s: Bronze Age oasis village · World Heritage
sites.te: The first farmers of the oasis
sites.se: Wheat, barley and dates were grown here 5,000 years ago beside a tomb for 600 people
sites.sa: زُرع القمح والشعير والتمر هنا قبل 5,000 عام إلى جانب قبر لستمئة إنسان
sites.desc: The Hili 8 settlement, dating to about 3000 BC, holds some of the earliest evidence of oasis agriculture in south-eastern Arabia (wheat, barley and date palm). The reconstructed Hili Grand Tomb of the Umm an-Nar culture is about 12 m in diameter and was originally about 4 m high; Tomb N, from the last two centuries of the 3rd millennium BC, held more than 600 burials. Aflaj irrigation channels dug in the first millennium BC are among the oldest known, and 3,000-year-old fingerprints of wall-builders were reported at Hili II in 2019. Part of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain, 17 locations inscribed in 2011 under criteria (iii), (iv) and (v), the UAE's first World Heritage property.
sites.sig: The clearest evidence of how farming, tower tombs and falaj irrigation began in the oases of eastern Arabia.
sites.ex: Danish, Iraqi and French missions from the 1960s; Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi
disc: Earliest oasis farming in south-east Arabia, c. 3000 BC
Iron Age aflaj among the oldest known
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Cultural Sites of Al Ain (Hafit, Hili, Bidaa Bint Saud and Oases Areas), ref. 1343, inscribed 2011.

sites.s: Beehive tombs of the Hafit period
sites.el: More than 500 cairns on the foothills near Mezyad
sites.se: Tombs on the mountain foothills hold pottery carried from Mesopotamia 5,000 years ago
sites.sa: قبور على سفوح الجبل تحوي فخارًا جُلب من بلاد الرافدين قبل 5,000 عام
sites.desc: More than 500 stone cairns on the foothills of Jebel Hafeet near Mezyad, first discovered in 1950 and excavated from 1962 by the Danish expedition. They date to 3200–2600 BC and give their name to the Hafit period, the start of the Bronze Age in the UAE. Imported Mesopotamian pottery of Jemdet Nasr type, about 5,000 years old, shows contact with the cities of Iraq. Part of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain, inscribed in 2011.
sites.sig: The earliest monumental tombs in the Emirates and the first evidence of long-distance trade with Mesopotamia.
sites.ex: Danish Archaeological Expedition, 1962; Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi
refs: Emirates Natural History Group (2011). The United Arab Emirates throughout the ages.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Cultural Sites of Al Ain, ref. 1343.

sites.s: 210,000 years of human presence · World Heritage
sites.te: The desert that kept people alive
sites.se: Eighteen layers of stone tools show humans returning here for 210,000 years
sites.sa: ثماني عشرة طبقة من الأدوات الحجرية تُظهر عودة الإنسان إلى هنا طوال 210,000 عام
sites.desc: A desert landscape of dunes, rocky outcrops and fossil remnants around Jebel Faya in central Sharjah, where 30 years of excavation by the Sharjah Archaeology Authority and international teams have uncovered 18 distinct layers of human activity spanning more than 210,000 years. A joint German–Emirati team led by Hans-Peter Uerpmann found handaxes, blades and points about 125,000 years old in 2011. Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025 as a cultural landscape, the first desert Palaeolithic site on the list and the only Arab-region site inscribed that year.
sites.sig: A key site for how early humans crossed and survived Arabia during the wet and dry phases of the last 200,000 years.
sites.ex: Sharjah Archaeology Authority with the University of Tübingen and other partners, 1990s onwards
refs: Current World Archaeology (2025). Faya Palaeolandscape becomes only site in the Arab world to be awarded UNESCO World Heritage status in 2025.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Faya Palaeolandscape, inscribed 2025.

sites.s: Capital of the kingdom of Uman · UNESCO tentative list
sites.se: A trading capital with horse burials, a mint and amphorae from Rhodes
sites.sa: عاصمة تجارية بمدافن خيول ودار سكّ وجرار من رودس
sites.desc: A town east of Jebel Faya, about 50 km from Sharjah, occupied from roughly 300 BC to 300 AD as the centre of the kingdom of Uman, probably the Omana of classical sources. Remains include a fort (the al-Husn building, 55 × 50 m), a buttressed palace, tower tombs and houses with underground kitchens; finds include horse and hybrid-camel burials with a gold bridle, coins imitating Alexander's tetradrachm with a coin mould, the largest number of Rhodian amphorae in Arabia, and a 2016 bilingual Aramaic–Hasaitic tombstone naming the kingdom. A 1994 cemetery held 26 graves, 12 for camels. Abandoned after a violent attack in the 3rd century AD; submitted to the UNESCO Tentative List in 2023.
sites.sig: The eponymous site of the late pre-Islamic period in south-east Arabia and proof of an Arabian kingdom trading with the Hellenistic world.
sites.ex: Iraqi mission 1973; Belgian and French missions from the 1980s; Sharjah Archaeology Authority
disc: Bilingual tombstone naming the kingdom of Uman (2016)
Horse burials with a gold bridle

sites.s: Neolithic herders’ cemetery
sites.se: Nomadic herders buried their dead here for a thousand years
sites.sa: دفن الرعاة الرُّحّل موتاهم هنا ألف عام
sites.desc: A limestone outcrop 48 km south-east of Sharjah city, rising to about 340 m, on the ridge that runs from Madam to Mleiha. The Neolithic cemetery BHS 18, dated by radiocarbon to about 5000–4000 BC, is one of the key Neolithic sites of southern Arabia; its burials are read as those of nomadic herders who came inland for the winter, and the whole site has yielded the complete remains of about 600 individuals. Hafit-period beehive graves, a unique clover-shaped Wadi Suq tomb (BHS 66), Iron Age burials and an Iron Age fort lie on the same mountain. Excavated by Iraqi, French, Spanish and, from 1995, University of Tübingen teams (ten seasons at BHS 18, 1996–2005).
sites.sig: The largest Neolithic cemetery in the region, with the best evidence for the health, diet and movements of Arabia's first herders.
sites.ex: University of Tübingen (H.-P. Uerpmann) with the Sharjah Directorate of Antiquities, 1995–2005

sites.s: Iron Age metal-working and ritual site
sites.el: Dune field at the edge of the Empty Quarter
sites.te: Snakes of copper in the dunes
sites.se: Smelting slag, arrowheads and copper snakes buried far from any ore
sites.sa: خبث صهر ورؤوس سهام وأفاعٍ نحاسية مدفونة بعيدًا عن أي خام
sites.desc: A site in the dunes of the Rub' al-Khali margin south of Dubai, excavated since 2002 by Jordanian, Australian, Spanish and Polish teams. Slag, ore nodules, crucibles and metallurgical tools show copper smelting and probably manufacture in Iron Age II, although no furnaces or moulds have yet been found; many copper arrowheads, axes and daggers were collected. The ritualised scattering of objects, with copper snakes, human figurines and soft-stone and alabaster vessels, suggests a ceremonial role. Location approximate.
sites.sig: A unique combination of industry and ritual in a place with no water or ore, still unexplained.
sites.ex: Dubai Municipality Architectural Heritage Department with Spanish (Sanisera), Australian (UNSW) and Polish (PCMA) teams, 2002 onwards
refs: Contreras Rodrigo, F. et al. (2017). Excavations in Area 2A at Sarūq al-Ḥadīd: Iron Age II evidence of copper production and ceremonial activities. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 47, 57–67.

sites.s: Oldest stone houses in the Gulf
sites.el: Island inside the Marawah Marine Biosphere Reserve
sites.se: An 8,000-year-old village with stone houses, burials and a pearl less than a centimetre long
sites.sa: قرية عمرها 8,000 عام ببيوت حجرية ومدافن ولؤلؤة أقصر من سنتيمتر
sites.desc: Excavations by the Abu Dhabi Islands Archaeological Survey began in March 1998 on Marawah Island and revealed a Stone Age village: fireplaces of Late Stone Age hunters, then stone houses about 7,500 years old, the earliest permanent stone buildings found in the Arabian Gulf, with burials inside former homes, tools, jewellery and fishing gear. Two more settlements, MR I and MR II, lie nearby. In 2019 a natural pearl less than a centimetre long, dated to 5800–5600 BC, was found, the oldest known anywhere, pushing pearling back nearly 8,000 years.
sites.sig: The oldest architecture and the oldest pearl of the Gulf, on one small island.
sites.ex: Abu Dhabi Islands Archaeological Survey (ADIAS) 1998–2004; Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi

sites.s: Church of the East monastery
sites.el: East coast of Sir Bani Yas Island
sites.se: A 1,400-year-old church and monastery that traded with its Muslim neighbours
sites.sa: كنيسة ودير عمرهما 1,400 عام تاجرا مع جيرانهما المسلمين
sites.desc: A church and monastery on the eastern coast of Sir Bani Yas Island, about 200 km from Abu Dhabi, found in 1992 and at first not recognised as religious. About 1,400 years old, it has dormitories, a kitchen, cells and burials, with more buildings found in 2014 to the west, south-west and north. Finds include Christian crosses and a decorative frieze now in the Louvre Abu Dhabi, and evidence that the monks kept cattle and fished and traded with Muslim neighbours in the 7th and 8th centuries. Opened to the public in 2019; the island also holds the Arabian Wildlife Park.
sites.sig: The only known Christian monastery in the UAE and a rare window on the Gulf at the dawn of Islam.
sites.ex: Abu Dhabi Islands Archaeological Survey (G. King) 1992–1996; Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi (P. Magee) 2014

sites.s: Hellenistic-period city and temple
sites.se: A coastal city whose temple named the sun god Shams in Aramaic
sites.sa: مدينة ساحلية سمّى معبدها إله الشمس «شمس» بالآرامية
sites.desc: One of the largest pre-Islamic sites in the Emirates, on the coast of Umm Al Quwain, partly excavated by an Iraqi mission in 1974 and by European missions from 1987. It belongs to the second phase of the Hellenistic period in the region; a Belgian team found a temple with three altars and an Aramaic inscription naming the solar deity Shams, together with imported glass and coins.
sites.sig: The main port of the Gulf coast in the early centuries AD, linking Mleiha inland to the Roman and Parthian world.
sites.ex: Iraqi mission 1974; Belgian, British, Danish and French missions 1987–1995

sites.s: Type site of the Umm an-Nar culture
sites.te: The island that named an age
sites.se: Fifty round tombs excavated by the Danes in 1959 gave a whole culture its name
sites.sa: خمسون قبرًا دائريًا نقّبها الدنماركيون عام 1959 أعطت ثقافة كاملة اسمها
sites.desc: A small island beside Abu Dhabi where a Danish expedition in 1959 excavated a cemetery of 50 above-ground circular tombs and a settlement of fishers and traders. The finds defined the Umm an-Nar period (2700–2000 BC), when the coast traded copper, pearls and pottery with Mesopotamia and the Indus. The island is now inside an industrial area and not open to visitors.
sites.sig: The reference site for the Bronze Age of the Emirates and Oman.
sites.ex: Danish Archaeological Expedition (P. V. Glob, G. Bibby), 1959–1965

sites.s: Medieval port of Ras Al Khaimah
sites.se: A trading town that shipped pearls and horses and imported porcelain from China
sites.sa: بلدة تجارية شحنت اللؤلؤ والخيول واستوردت الخزف من الصين
sites.desc: The medieval port of Julfar, prominent in trade by the early 14th century and described by Duarte Barbosa in 1517, is now placed at Kush in the Shimal plain north of Ras Al Khaimah city; its oldest remains date to the 13th century. Excavations uncovered Chinese and East Asian porcelain among the houses of a town that traded pearls and horses across the Indian Ocean. Location approximate.
sites.sig: The Emirates' main link to the Indian Ocean trade of the Middle Ages, and the home port of the navigator Ahmad ibn Majid.
sites.ex: British (Kennet), Japanese, French and German missions, 1970s–1990s
refs: Emirates Natural History Group (2011). The United Arab Emirates throughout the ages.

sites.s: Folded Eocene mountain
sites.dr: Rocks 56 – 16 million years old; folded 28 – 15 million years ago
sites.se: A 26 km fold with one side tipped over, hot springs at its foot
sites.sa: طيّة بطول 26 كم انقلب أحد جانبيها، وينابيع حارة عند قدمها
sites.desc: An isolated mountain of 1,249 m on the UAE–Oman border near Al Ain, 26 km long and 4–5 km wide, trending NNW–SSE. It is an asymmetric anticline of shallow-marine limestone, marl and evaporite with corals, foraminifera and bryozoa, ranging from early Eocene in the core to early Miocene on the flanks; the west limb dips about 30° and the east limb is overturned at about 70°, probably over a backthrust, with folding dated to the late Oligocene to middle Miocene. Hot springs of about 40 °C at Green Mubazzarah come from water circulating 2 km down through faults beneath the fold. Caves reach at least 150 m. About 500 Hafit-period tombs lie on its foothills.
sites.sig: The UAE's best-exposed anticline, the source of Al Ain's hot springs and the backdrop to its oldest tombs.
sites.ex: Geological surveys of the UAE (Ministry of Energy / British Geological Survey)

sites.s: Cretaceous sea floor on show
sites.dr: Rocks at least 93 million years old
sites.se: Ammonites and sea urchins from a sea that covered Sharjah 93 million years ago
sites.sa: أمونيتات وقنافذ بحر من بحر غطّى الشارقة قبل 93 مليون عام
sites.desc: A visitor park opened on 21 January 2020 on the limestone ridge of Jebel Buhais, displaying fossils and features dating back at least 93 million years to the Cretaceous, when the area lay beneath a shallow sea before the Hajar Mountains rose. The ridge runs almost continuously from Madam to Mleiha and also carries the Neolithic to Iron Age cemeteries of Jebel Buhais.
sites.sig: The easiest place in the UAE to see the marine rocks that predate the ophiolite and the mountains.
sites.ex: Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority

sites.s: Tallest dune in the UAE
sites.se: A 300 m dune at the edge of the Empty Quarter, 1.6 km long
sites.sa: كثيب بارتفاع 300 م على حافة الربع الخالي، طوله 1.6 كم
sites.desc: A dune about 300 m high and 1,600 m long with a slip face reported at 50°, about 25 km south of Liwa Oasis and 250 km from Abu Dhabi, at the northern edge of the Rub' al Khali (Empty Quarter). The tallest dune in the UAE, it hosts the Liwa Moreeb Dune Festival of hill-climb racing. The dunes of Liwa are the end of a sand sea that stretches across southern Arabia.
sites.sig: The UAE's doorway to the largest sand desert on Earth.
sites.ex: Abu Dhabi Department of Culture and Tourism (Liwa festival)
refs: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Moreeb Dune, citing Liwa Sports Club and Visit Abu Dhabi.

sites.s: Mountain park on ancient ocean crust · World Heritage 2026
sites.te: Water in the mountains of the sea floor
sites.se: Springs and tahr on rocks that were once ocean crust, 90 million years old
sites.sa: ينابيع ووعول على صخور كانت يومًا قشرة محيط عمرها 90 مليون عام
sites.desc: A 225 km² park in the Hajar Mountains of Fujairah with more than 300 springs and 60 streams, designated the UAE's first mountain protected area in 2009 and inscribed on the World Heritage List at the 2026 session in Busan as the country's first natural site. Its rocks are ophiolite, fragments of oceanic crust about 90 million years old considered among the best preserved in the world. Surveys since 2006 have recorded 1,099 species, including the endangered Arabian tahr (one of its three remaining habitats), the Arabian caracal rediscovered in 2025, Blanford's fox and a dragonfly once thought extinct.
sites.sig: The UAE's richest mountain ecosystem and its first natural World Heritage site, on a slice of the ocean floor.
sites.ex: Fujairah Environment Authority with Emirates Nature–WWF, 2006 onwards
refs: Scene Traveller (26 July 2026). Wadi Wurayah becomes UAE's first UNESCO natural World Heritage site.

sites.s: Flamingo breeding wetland · Ramsar
sites.se: Up to 3,600 flamingos on lakes fed by treated city water
sites.sa: حتى 3,600 طائر فلامنغو على بحيرات تغذّيها مياه المدينة المعالجة
sites.desc: A 5 km² wetland of lakes and sabkha south-east of Abu Dhabi city, declared a reserve in 1998 and the emirate's first Ramsar site in 2013, with water levels partly maintained by tertiary-treated wastewater. Greater flamingos first bred successfully in December 1998, fledging 10 young in April 1999, and have bred every year since 2011; January counts in 2013–2018 ranged from 2,500 to 3,600 birds. Recorded diversity: 236 bird, 39 plant, 15 reptile, 10 mammal and 354 invertebrate species, about 21% of the emirate's terrestrial species. Visitors rose from 2,560 in 2014–15 to 5,780 in 2017–18.
sites.sig: The first regular flamingo breeding site in the Gulf states and a model of a wetland made with recycled water.
sites.ex: Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi
refs: Campbell, O., Javed, S., Al Dhaheri, S. et al. (2018). Al Wathba Wetland Reserve, Abu Dhabi emirate: successful mixing of birds and people. Sandgrouse Supplement 4.

sites.s: Flamingos at the end of Dubai Creek · Ramsar
sites.se: Twenty thousand waterbirds winter in a lagoon ringed by the city
sites.sa: عشرون ألف طائر مائي تشتو في بحيرة تحيط بها المدينة
sites.desc: A 620 ha sanctuary of mangrove, lagoon, intertidal mud and sand flats and saline flats at the end of the 14 km Dubai Creek, designated a Ramsar site on 29 August 2007. More than 20,000 waterbirds of 67 species winter here, including more than 3,000 greater flamingos; more than 1% of the regional population of broad-billed sandpipers passes through, and the threatened sociable lapwing and greater spotted eagle occur. Over 450 animal and 47 plant species are recorded, and about 10,000 people visit each year.
sites.sig: A wetland of international importance surviving inside one of the fastest-growing cities on Earth.
sites.ex: Dubai Municipality (Environment Department)
refs: Ramsar Sites Information Service. Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary (site 1715), designated 2007.

sites.s: Oldest mangrove woodland in the region · Ramsar
sites.se: Tall old mangroves where a kingfisher found nowhere else in the world breeds
sites.sa: قرم عالٍ عتيق يتكاثر فيه رفراف لا يوجد في أي مكان آخر في العالم
sites.desc: A 1,494 ha protected area on the Gulf of Oman coast of Sharjah near the Oman border, listed under Ramsar on 10 March 2013. Its Avicennia marina trees are the tallest and the most extensive mature mangrove woodland in the biogeographic region. The Kalba white-collared kingfisher (Todiramphus chloris kalbaensis), an endemic subspecies, breeds almost exclusively here; Sykes's warbler has one of its two regional breeding sites; hawksbill and green turtles enter the creeks at high tide to feed. Habitats also include beach, tidal channels, salt marsh and Acacia woodland.
sites.sig: A relict mangrove forest that holds a bird found nowhere else on Earth.
sites.ex: Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority
refs: Ramsar Sites Information Service. Mangrove and Al Hafeya Protected Area in Khor Kalba (site 2125), designated 2013.

sites.n: Marawah Marine Biosphere Reserve and Bu Tinah
sites.s: Densest dugong population in the world
sites.el: Shallow seagrass banks west of Abu Dhabi
sites.se: Abu Dhabi’s seagrass holds the second-largest dugong population after Australia
sites.sa: تحتضن أعشاب أبوظبي البحرية ثاني أكبر تجمّع للأطوم بعد أستراليا
sites.desc: The UAE's first UNESCO biosphere reserve, recognised in 2007, covering seagrass beds, coral reefs and mangroves around Marawah Island west of Abu Dhabi, with four turtle species and 70 fish species. The Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi protects about 3,000 dugongs, mostly in Marawah and the Al Yasat protected area, the largest population after Australia; Bu Tinah, inside the reserve, is described as the densest dugong population in the world. Dugongs have been studied here since 1999 by aerial survey, satellite tagging and genetics; threats are abandoned nets, habitat loss, pollution and boat strikes.
sites.sig: The most important dugong habitat outside Australia.
sites.ex: Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi, 1999 onwards
disc: About 3,000 dugongs in Abu Dhabi waters
Bu Tinah: densest dugong population known

sites.s: Bronze–Iron Age mound and Umm an-Nar fortress tower · excavated since 1989
sites.p: Umm an-Nar, Wadi Suq and Iron Age
sites.se: A four-hectare mound on the Sharjah–Umm Al Quwain line with the largest Umm an-Nar fortress tower in the UAE and a tomb of about 410 people
sites.sa: تلّ بمساحة أربعة هكتارات على خط الشارقة وأم القيوين يضم أكبر برج حصن من حضارة أم النار في الإمارات ومدفناً لنحو 410 أشخاص
sites.desc: Tell Abraq is a settlement mound of about four hectares rising roughly 10 m above the sabkha, described as the best preserved and largest prehistoric settlement in the lower Arabian Gulf. A circular mud-brick fortress faced with stone, about 40 m in diameter and 8 m high, was built around 2200 BC (charcoal dated 2461–2199 BC), with a stone-lined well at its centre. An Umm an-Nar tomb about 6 m across, 10 m west of the tower, held the commingled remains of about 410 individuals, including a young woman with polio. Occupation ran from c. 2200 BC to AD 200, and finds include Harappan weights, Barbar pottery, Bactrian ivory and more than 100,000 animal bones, the largest faunal assemblage in the Arabian Peninsula.
sites.sig: The site's long sequence defined the Iron Age I–III chronology of the UAE and shows the region's trade with Mesopotamia, Iran, Bahrain and the Indus.
sites.ex: University of Copenhagen (D.T. Potts, 1989–1998); Bryn Mawr College and University of Tübingen (P. Magee, from 2007); Italian Archaeological Mission in Umm al-Quwain (M. Degli Esposti, from 2019)

sites.s: Largest pre-Islamic site in Ras Al Khaimah · c. 250 tombs and a hilltop fort
sites.p: Umm an-Nar to Wadi Suq, with a medieval fort
sites.el: Tomb Sh 222: 11.3 m across, about 300 burials
sites.te: A city of the dead below the mountains
sites.se: About 250 monumental tombs at the foot of the mountains north of Ras Al Khaimah, settled for at least 4,500 years, with a medieval fort on the outcrop above
sites.sa: نحو 250 مدفناً ضخماً عند سفح الجبال شمال رأس الخيمة، استُوطن المكان منذ 4,500 سنة على الأقل، ويعلوه حصن من العصور الوسطى
sites.desc: Shimal, about 8 km north-east of Ras Al Khaimah town, is the largest pre-Islamic site in the emirate and has been settled for at least 4,500 years. Its cemetery holds about 250 tombs of several types, many monumental: the Umm an-Nar tomb Sh 222 is 11.3 m across and held about 300 burials dated to c. 2200–2000 BC, while Wadi Suq tombs such as Sh 99 (16 m long, at least 66 individuals) and Sh 102 (about 140 individuals, 15th–13th centuries BC) date to the 2nd millennium BC. Finds include soft-stone vessels, bronze and copper weapons, beads and pottery possibly imported from Bahrain and south-eastern Iran. On the outcrop above the village stands the so-called 'Palace of the Queen of Sheba', a fortification probably no older than Julfar (14th–18th centuries AD).
sites.sig: Shimal is the type site for the Wadi Suq period in the northern Emirates and shows continuous settlement from the Bronze Age to the Islamic era.
sites.ex: British and German archaeologists since 1976, chiefly a team from the University of Göttingen in the mid-1980s; finds in the National Museum of Ras Al Khaimah
disc: Cemetery of about 250 tombs, some holding over 300 burials

sites.s: Late antique monastery and the oldest known pearling town in the Arabian Gulf
sites.te: Pearls before the dawn of Islam
sites.se: A monastery found in 2022 and a town of hundreds of beach-rock houses, pearls and the oldest well-dated diver's weight in the Emirates
sites.sa: دير اكتُشف عام 2022 وبلدة من مئات البيوت المبنية بحجر الشاطئ، مع لآلئ وأقدم ثقل غواص مؤرخ في الإمارات
sites.desc: On Al Sinniyah Island in the Umm Al Quwain lagoon, archaeologists announced in March 2023 the oldest pearling town yet found in the Arabian Gulf, covering about 12 hectares with hundreds of houses and several thousand residents. The town was occupied for about 200 years, from the late 6th or early 7th century to the mid-8th century AD, and sits beside a Christian monastery unearthed in 2022 and dated to the 7th–8th centuries. Excavations found pearls, a pearl diver's weight described as the earliest well-dated example in the Emirates, a 6th–7th century Sasanian stamp seal, oyster-shell middens of possibly millions of shells and ceramics of which about 12% were imported from India. Large courtyard houses of merchants stood among small one- or two-room houses of fishermen, all built of local beach rock.
sites.sig: The island shows that pearling towns and Christian communities flourished in the Gulf a generation before Islam and continued for two generations after it.

sites.s: Abbasid caravan town inside modern Dubai · managed by Dubai Culture
sites.te: A caravan city under the villas
sites.se: An 80,000 m² Abbasid trading settlement with a mosque, caravanserai, souq and ruler's house, first excavated in 1969
sites.sa: مستوطنة تجارية عباسية بمساحة 80,000 م² تضم مسجداً وخاناً وسوقاً وبيت الحاكم، بدأ تنقيبها عام 1969
sites.desc: The Jumeirah Archaeological Site is a fenced plot of about 80,000 m² (8 ha) in Jumeirah 2, Dubai, preserving the remains of a trading settlement of the Abbasid period, around the 10th century AD. It was first explored in 1969 by Dimitri Baramki of the American University of Beirut, continued by an Iraqi team in 1974, and has been excavated by Dubai's own department since 1993. Seven structures have been identified, including a mosque, a caravanserai, a souq, a workshop and a large residential building believed to be the ruler's house, along a caravan route linking India and China with Oman and Iraq. Finds include Abbasid coins, glazed pottery from southern Iraq, Chinese stoneware and stucco decoration; the site is owned and managed by the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority.
sites.sig: It is the main physical evidence that an organised Islamic trading town existed in the Dubai area a thousand years ago.

sites.s: Highest hilltop fort in the UAE · Bronze Age hill, 1819 siege
sites.p: Late Bronze Age settlement; 18th–19th century fort
sites.se: A mud-brick fort on a 70 m hill above Rams where about 400 people held out for three days in December 1819 before the General Maritime Treaty
sites.sa: قلعة من الطوب الطيني على تل بارتفاع 70 متراً فوق رمس صمد فيها نحو 400 شخص ثلاثة أيام في ديسمبر 1819 قبل المعاهدة البحرية العامة
sites.desc: Dhayah Fort stands on a twin-peaked hill about 70 m high between the date gardens and the Jebel Jais mountains in Ras Al Khaimah and is described as the highest hilltop fort in the UAE. The hill was used for settlement and fortification in the Late Bronze Age (c. 1600–1300 BC), and twelve Wadi Suq tombs of c. 2000–1300 BC lie at its base, four of them excavated. In December 1819 a British landing force marched inland and bombarded the fort with mortars and two 24-pounder cannons dragged four miles from the coast; about 400 people held out for three days without water before surrendering at 10:30 on 22 December, after which the fort was demolished. The present fort was rebuilt after 1819 and restored in the late 1990s, and the fall of Dhayah paved the way for the General Maritime Treaty of 1820.
sites.sig: Dhayah links a Bronze Age hill settlement with the 1819 events that reshaped the political history of the Gulf coast.

sites.s: Hafit tombs and Iron Age falaj · World Heritage (Al Ain, 2011)
sites.el: Iron Age hall 10 × 13 m with 12 columns
sites.se: A rocky outcrop north of Al Ain with 5,000-year-old tombs and one of the earliest falaj irrigation systems known, with a mud-brick water house
sites.sa: نتوء صخري شمال العين يضم مدافن عمرها 5,000 سنة وواحداً من أقدم أنظمة الأفلاج المعروفة مع بيت طيني لتوزيع الماء
sites.desc: Bidaa Bint Saud lies about 15–25 km north of Al Ain, where the outcrop of Garn bin Saud rises about 40 m above a probable caravan route. Collapsed domed tombs of the Hafit period (3200–2600 BC) line the eastern face, alongside Wadi Suq burials and Iron Age collective graves that yielded pottery, stone vessels, dagger blades, bronze arrowheads and beads. Two Iron Age falaj channels have been partly excavated, with sandstone-lined shafts, a stepped underground access and a large open cistern; pottery dating places the falaj before the Achaemenid Empire, supporting a south-east Arabian origin for the system. Beside the falaj stands a mud-brick building with a 10 × 13 m hall, walls up to 160 cm high and 12 columns, probably a water distribution point. The site is part of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2011.
sites.sig: Its Iron Age falaj is key evidence that underground irrigation was invented in south-east Arabia rather than imported from Persia.

sites.s: Highest peak in the UAE, 1,934 m · Hajar Mountains
sites.se: A 1,934 m limestone summit in the Hajar range raised when the Arabian and Eurasian plates collided in the late Cretaceous
sites.sa: قمة جيرية بارتفاع 1,934 متراً في سلسلة الحجر ارتفعت عندما اصطدمت الصفيحتان العربية والأوراسية في أواخر العصر الطباشيري
sites.desc: Jebel Jais in Ras Al Khaimah rises to 1,934 m above sea level and is the highest peak in the United Arab Emirates. It belongs to the Al Hajar range, about 700 km long and 100 km wide across the UAE and Oman, whose jagged peaks were shaped by continental collision along the Arabian–Eurasian plate boundary in the late Cretaceous. The mountain contains marine and terrestrial sedimentary rocks with fossils, and the range holds ophiolites, among the few places where oceanic rocks can be studied on land; its formations are more than 70 million years old. The summit road leads to the UAE's highest viewing deck park, and the Jais Flight zipline is 2.83 km long.
sites.sig: It is the highest point of the Emirates and the clearest window on the uplift of the Hajar Mountains.

sites.s: Marine limestone ridge full of Cretaceous fossils · Mleiha National Park
sites.p: Late Cretaceous – Paleocene marine limestone over the Samail Ophiolite
sites.el: Shells, snails, clams and sea urchins in the rock
sites.te: A sea floor lifted into the desert
sites.se: A limestone ridge north of Jebel Faya packed with snail, clam and sea-urchin fossils from a shallow sea more than 80 million years ago
sites.sa: حافة جيرية شمال جبل الفاية تمتلئ بأحافير القواقع والمحار وقنافذ البحر من بحر ضحل قبل أكثر من 80 مليون سنة
sites.desc: Fossil Rock lies a few kilometres north of Jebel Faya in Sharjah, beside the limestone ridge of Jebel Maleihah at the northern edge of the Rub' al Khali. The ridges are marine limestone deposited over tens of millions of years from the Late Cretaceous to the early–mid Paleocene on top of the Samail Ophiolite, one of the world's largest exposures of ancient oceanic crust thrust onto Arabia. Coral fragments and marine invertebrate fossils are visible throughout, and Fossil Rock itself holds an abundance of snail, clam and sea-urchin remains more than 80 million years old. Nearby Jebel Faya stands 412 m above sea level, and the surrounding Faya Palaeolandscape was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025.
sites.sig: It is the most accessible place in the UAE to see a Cretaceous sea floor and the ophiolite beneath it.

sites.s: Seven-million-year-old elephant footprints · Baynunah Formation, Al Dhafra
sites.el: Single trackway 260 m long over 5 hectares
sites.te: A herd walks across the mud
sites.se: Hundreds of fossil footprints of a herd of four-tusked elephant ancestors, with a lone male's 260 m trail, on a 5-hectare plain in western Abu Dhabi
sites.sa: مئات من آثار أقدام متحجرة لقطيع من أسلاف الفيلة ذات الأنياب الأربعة، مع مسار ذكر منفرد بطول 260 متراً، على سهل مساحته 5 هكتارات غرب أبوظبي
sites.desc: Mleisa 1, in the Al Dhafra region of western Abu Dhabi, preserves hundreds of elephant footprints in the Baynunah Formation, dated to about seven million years ago in the Late Miocene. A solitary male's trackway runs 260 m, while other tracks were left by herding females and juveniles; the site covers about 5 hectares and is one of the largest trackway sites in the world. The 2012 study in Biology Letters by an international team including Faysal Bibi, Brian Kraatz and Andrew Hill used stride lengths to show a herd of adults and a young calf. The Baynunah Formation, laid down by a braided river system with channels three metres deep, has also yielded four-tusked elephants, a primitive hippopotamus, giraffes, six antelope species, crocodiles, turtles, monkeys and ostriches; five further elephant trackway sites have since been found in Al Dhafra.
sites.sig: It is the oldest direct evidence of herd behaviour in elephant ancestors and shows a wooded, river-crossed Arabia seven million years ago.

sites.s: World type locality of the sabkha · Holocene carbonate–evaporite flats
sites.el: Salt flats up to 15 km wide
sites.te: The salt flats that wrote the textbooks
sites.se: The coastal salt flats west of Abu Dhabi, the world's reference sabkha since Graham Evans found anhydrite forming just below their surface in the 1960s
sites.sa: السبخات الساحلية غرب أبوظبي، المرجع العالمي للسبخات منذ أن وجد غراهام إيفانز الأنهيدريت يتكوّن تحت سطحها في الستينيات
sites.desc: The coast of Abu Dhabi is the accepted type locality for sabkhas: a shallow carbonate ramp with a tidal range of 1–2 m where salt flats cover about 36,000 km² and extend up to 15 km inland from dune fields. Groundwater lies never deeper than 1.5 m and is concentrated to about ten times seawater, precipitating calcite, dolomite and gypsum with lesser anhydrite, halite and carnallite; net evaporation has averaged 6 cm a year over the last 4,000–5,000 years and the flats prograde about 1 m per 1,000 years. Prof Graham Evans of Imperial College London first documented the flats in 1962 and found anhydrite forming just below the surface at Saadiyat and Musaffah, a discovery now in geology textbooks. His associate Dr Tony Kirkham identified a 30 km stretch of coast at Al Dabbiya as of exceptional significance and campaigned for protection from infilling and industry.
sites.sig: These flats are the global reference for how evaporite minerals form in arid coasts and a gauge of past sea-level change.

sites.s: More than 1,700 cemented Ice Age dunes · protected area opened 2022
sites.se: Cross-bedded sand cemented by calcium carbonate from rising groundwater, then carved by wind into 1,700 frozen dunes east of Abu Dhabi
sites.sa: رمال متقاطعة الطبقات لحمتها كربونات الكالسيوم من المياه الجوفية الصاعدة ثم نحتتها الرياح إلى 1,700 كثيب متحجر شرق أبوظبي
sites.desc: The Al Wathba Fossil Dunes Protected Area, 45 km east of Abu Dhabi and south of the Al Wathba Wetland Reserve, covers about 7 km² and contains more than 1,700 lightly cemented, cross-bedded sand outcrops. The Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi dates them to about 120,000–150,000 years ago: sand blew in from the exposed bed of the Arabian Gulf during dry glacial periods, rising groundwater then cemented it with calcium carbonate, and wind carved the hardened sand into its present shapes. Prof Thomas Steuber of Khalifa University, who studied the dunes, notes that generations of dunes formed in ice-age cycles between about 200,000 and 7,000 years ago and that wind will eventually destroy them. The site opened free to the public in 2022 as an IUCN category III geological reserve and has been nominated for UNESCO's Global Geoparks list.
sites.sig: The dunes record the Gulf's dry glacial sea floor and the climate swings of the last ice ages.

sites.s: 225 km² national park · about 800 Arabian oryx
sites.te: Oryx on five percent of Dubai
sites.ta: المها على خمسة بالمئة من دبي
sites.se: A fenced reserve of 225 km² where 70 reintroduced Arabian oryx grew to about 800, with gazelles, houbara and more than 560 recorded species
sites.sa: محمية مسوّرة بمساحة 225 كم² تكاثر فيها 70 مهاً عربياً أُعيد توطينها إلى نحو 800، مع الغزلان والحبارى وأكثر من 560 نوعاً مسجلاً
sites.desc: The Dubai Desert Conservation Reserve covers 225 km², almost 5% of Dubai's land area, about 40 km from the city. It began in 1999 around the 27 km² Al Maha resort and was proclaimed a national park and protected area in 2003, run under the Dubai Conservation Board with a team of 15 conservation officers; domestic livestock were removed in 2008. The reserve reintroduced 70 Arabian oryx and now holds about 800, the largest free-roaming herd in the UAE, with 171 relocated to other reserves, plus about 200 sand gazelles, 420 mountain gazelles and 2,800 reintroduced houbara bustards. Surveys record 18 mammal, 142 bird, 26 reptile, more than 300 arthropod and 74 native plant species across gravel plains, sand dunes and valley dunes.
sites.sig: It shows how a fenced desert reserve can rebuild a herd of a species once extinct in the wild.

sites.s: Largest coral reef in the UAE · 55 km² protected area
sites.el: About 40% of Arabian Gulf coral species
sites.te: The reef that survived the heat
sites.se: A long reef strip near Ghantoot, the most extensive reef on the Gulf side of the UAE, home to turtles, dugongs, sea snakes and clownfish
sites.sa: شريط مرجاني طويل قرب غنتوت، أوسع شعاب على ساحل الخليج العربي في الإمارات، تعيش فيه السلاحف والأطوم وثعابين البحر وسمك المهرج
sites.desc: Ras Ghanada, near Ghantoot about 90 km north-east of Abu Dhabi city, is a long, narrow reef strip running parallel to the mainland for several kilometres. Dr John Burt of New York University Abu Dhabi calls it the most extensive reef on the Arabian Gulf side of the UAE, and EWS-WWF described it in 2007 as the best and healthiest reef in Abu Dhabi; Burt has monitored it with the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi since 2010 using fish counts and seafloor photographs every three metres. The 1996–98 El Niño killed about 90% of Gulf corals, and the reef lies close to the breakwater of Khalifa Port, opened in 2012. The Ras Ghanadah Protected Area now covers 55 km² and holds about 40% of the coral species of the Arabian Gulf, with turtles, dugongs, sea snakes and clownfish.
sites.sig: It is the UAE's largest coral reef and a natural laboratory for corals living in the world's hottest sea.

sites.s: Tidal lagoon of Umm Al Quwain · Important Bird Area
sites.el: Up to 4,000 lesser sand plovers in winter
sites.se: An unprotected tidal lagoon around Al Sinniyah Island that hosts 350–450 wintering crab plovers, endangered great knots and thousands of sand plovers
sites.sa: خور مدّي غير محمي حول جزيرة السينية يستضيف 350–450 زقزاق سرطان شاتياً وطيور القطقاط الكبير المهددة وآلاف الزقزاقات الرملية
sites.desc: Khor Al Beidah is a tidal wetland of mudflats, sandflats and mangrove in the Emirate of Umm Al Quwain, listed as an Important Bird Area by BirdLife International and the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment in 2017. Counts from 2010–2015 recorded 350–450 wintering crab plovers, 1,700–4,000 lesser sand plovers, 850–2,000 greater sand plovers, 1,000–2,000 Kentish plovers, 210–310 western reef egrets and 60–88 endangered great knots. More than 420 bird species have been recorded in the region, but less than 10% of the site is covered by any protected designation and BirdLife rates the pressure as high, from biological resource use and likely residential and commercial development. Illegal cutting of mangroves has been reported.
sites.sig: It is one of the most important shorebird wintering lagoons on the UAE's Gulf coast and still lacks formal protection.

sites.s: Mangrove lagoon of Ajman · Ramsar wetland, protected since 2004
sites.se: A 195-hectare mangrove and lagoon reserve at the mouth of Ajman Creek with pink flamingos and over 50 other bird species, the UAE's seventh Ramsar site
sites.sa: محمية قرم وبحيرات بمساحة 195 هكتاراً عند مصب خور عجمان تزورها طيور النحام الوردي وأكثر من 50 نوعاً آخر من الطيور، وهي سابع موقع رامسار في الإمارات
sites.desc: Al Zorah Nature Reserve covers 195 hectares straddling the mouth of the one-kilometre-long Ajman Creek, with mangroves, sandy beaches, salt flats and lagoons. Legally protected since 2004, it was declared a Wetland of International Importance in 2018, the seventh Ramsar site in the UAE, with 108 recorded animal species including birds, fish, corals and molluscs. Large numbers of pink flamingos gather at certain times of year alongside more than 50 other bird species, and the mangroves are among the few remaining in the northern Emirates. On 24 November 2023, 6,600 mangrove saplings were planted over 0.9 hectares in a restoration project with Emirates Nature–WWF.
sites.sig: It is the main surviving mangrove wetland of Ajman and shows a small emirate protecting its creek amid urban growth.

sites.se: Grey mangrove channels on the eastern edge of Abu Dhabi city, about 10 km² and some three-quarters of the UAE's mangrove forest, with flamingos, herons and turtles
sites.sa: قنوات القرم الرمادي على الطرف الشرقي لمدينة أبوظبي بمساحة نحو 10 كم²، أي نحو ثلاثة أرباع غابات القرم في الإمارات، مع طيور النحام والبلشون والسلاحف
sites.desc: The Mangrove National Park lies along the Eastern Mangroves corniche of Abu Dhabi city and covers about 10 km², described by Aletihad as about 75% of the UAE's total mangrove forest area and protected by the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi. The forest is grey mangrove, Avicennia marina, locally called qurm, which grows 2–4 m tall in the intertidal zone; it absorbs carbon, purifies water and buffers tidal surges. Greater flamingos, western reef herons, crabs, turtles, foxes, dugongs and dolphins are recorded, and visitors explore by boardwalk, kayak and eco-boat. Sheikh Zayed began mangrove restoration in the 1970s; the UAE now has about 60 million mangrove trees over roughly 200 km² and aims for 100 million by 2030.
sites.sig: It is the largest urban mangrove forest in the Emirates and the heart of the country's mangrove-planting ambition.

sites.desc: A marine national park off Saadiyat Island in Abu Dhabi, declared in 2017 and covering 59 km². It includes about 7 km² of coral reefs and 8 km² of seagrass. Recorded fauna include 24 bird, 13 reptile and 5 mammal species, 28 of them threatened, among them dolphins, green turtles, sea snakes and the critically endangered hawksbill turtle. sites.desc: This record groups four of Dubai's eight protected areas: Al Marmoom Desert Conservation Reserve, Al Wohoosh Desert Conservation Reserve, Jabal Nazwa Conservation Reserve and Ghaf Nazwa Conservation Reserve. Their boundaries were set by a decree of the Ruler of Dubai announced in May 2014, and Dubai Municipality manages them; the eight reserves cover about 31% of the emirate. Al Marmoom was launched in January 2018 as the UAE's first unfenced conservation reserve, covering about 10% of Dubai, with the Al Qudra lakes, 26 reptile, 9 mammal and 39 plant species and flocks of 300 to 500 flamingos. The reserves were set up to protect desert plants such as samar, ghaf and sidr.
sites.sig: Dubai's inland reserves keep large tracts of desert, ghaf woodland and desert lakes protected next to a fast-growing city.

sites.s: Ramsar mudflats west of Musaffah · flamingo breeding record and threatened turtles
sites.ta: حيث عشّش ألفا زوج من الفلامنغو
sites.se: Tidal mudflats near Abu Dhabi where flamingos once raised 801 chicks and more than 80 kinds of birds feed
sites.sa: سهول طينية مدّية قرب أبوظبي فقس فيها ذات مرة 801 فرخ فلامنغو، وتقتات فيها أكثر من 80 نوعًا من الطيور
sites.desc: A coastal wetland of 14,504.5 ha west of the Musaffah channel, about 20 km from Abu Dhabi city, designated as Ramsar site no. 2293 on 27 September 2016. Habitats include mangroves, salt marshes, seagrass beds and tidal mudflats that support more than 80 migratory and resident bird species. In 2009 it hosted a record greater flamingo breeding event of 2,000 pairs and 801 hatchlings. Threatened species include hawksbill and green turtles, greater spotted eagle, Socotra cormorant and dugong.
sites.sig: One of the Arabian Gulf's key flamingo breeding wetlands, beside a major industrial city.

sites.dr: Dubai reserve 2014; Ramsar site no. 2368, 9 January 2019
sites.se: In the Hajar Mountains of Hatta, rare freshwater pools shelter dragonflies, fish and amphibians, while Arabian tahr live on the slopes
sites.sa: في جبال الحجر بحتا تؤوي برك المياه العذبة النادرة اليعاسيب والأسماك والبرمائيات، فيما يعيش الطهر العربي على السفوح
sites.desc: A 2,100 ha reserve in the Hajar Mountains of Dubai, part of the Oman–UAE ophiolite, designated as Ramsar site no. 2368 on 9 January 2019. It is a rare mountain freshwater ecosystem; the mountains receive about 30% of the country's annual rainfall, recharging the aquifer that feeds the Hatta and Al Ghabra dams. The site supports 19% of the country's plant species, 79% of its dragonfly species, 27% of its bird species and 44% of its mammal species. Threatened species include the Arabian leopard, Arabian tahr and Egyptian vulture.
sites.sig: A rare freshwater mountain wetland that concentrates much of the UAE's biodiversity in a small area.

sites.se: Between Palm Jebel Ali and Abu Dhabi, the only beaches in Dubai where hawksbill turtles still lay their eggs

sites.desc: A 2,002 ha coastal and marine sanctuary from Palm Jebel Ali south-west to the Abu Dhabi border, designated as Ramsar site no. 2364 on 25 October 2018 and part of the Jabal Ali Marine Sanctuary, an Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Area under the CBD. Habitats include coral reefs, mangroves, shallow lagoons, seagrass and oyster beds and sandy shores, sheltering over 500 marine species. Its beaches are the only hawksbill turtle breeding grounds in the emirate, with 30 nests recorded in 2017. Seagrass beds feed green turtles and dugongs.

sites.s: Ramsar inland wetland in Sharjah · a former tidal lagoon with 144 bird species
sites.dr: Sharjah reserve 2007; Ramsar site no. 2386, 9 May 2019
sites.te: A lagoon left behind by the sea
sites.se: Once a tidal lagoon, Wasit is now an inland wetland in Sharjah where at least 144 kinds of birds have been seen
sites.sa: كانت واسط بحيرة مدّية، وهي اليوم أرض رطبة داخلية في الشارقة رُصد فيها ما لا يقل عن 144 نوعًا من الطيور
sites.desc: An 86 ha inland lake and wetland complex about 15 km from the coast and Sharjah city, designated as Ramsar site no. 2386 on 9 May 2019. It was once a tidal lagoon, which makes it useful for understanding how the coastline has changed. Mudflats, lakes, dunes, reed beds and thickets support at least 144 bird species, many of them migrants, including near-threatened curlew sandpiper, bar-tailed and black-tailed godwits and Eurasian curlew, and the vulnerable Socotra cormorant. It was designated a protected area by the Ruler of Sharjah in 2007.
sites.sig: A rare urban-edge wetland that records the former shoreline of Sharjah.

sites.s: Mountain tombs, villages and falaj of Hatta · Bronze Age to Islamic periods
sites.el: Over 70 tombs at Jabal al Yamh
sites.se: Above Hatta, more than seventy stone tombs line the ridge, and below them lie old stone villages and a water channel 560 m long
sites.sa: فوق حتا تصطف على الجبل أكثر من سبعين مدفنًا حجريًا، وتحتها قرى حجرية قديمة وقناة فلج يبلغ طولها نحو 560 مترًا
sites.desc: A UNESCO Tentative List property (2023) in the Hatta enclave of Dubai, where 22 archaeological sites have been identified, documented and mapped. The Jabal al Yamh necropolis has over 70 tombs spread over about 4 km, mostly in the Hafit style with others of Umm an-Nar, Wadi Suq and Iron Age type, some reused into the Middle Islamic period. Suhaila 1 was occupied from the early Islamic era to the mid-20th century, while Suhaila 2 and Wadi Jeema are larger settlements with agricultural terraces. An underground falaj about 560 m long dates to the 1st millennium BCE.
sites.sig: A mountain landscape showing continuous use of the Hajar valleys from the Early Bronze Age to the recent past.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 6664

sites.s: Traditional merchants' harbour · dhows, abras, souqs and wind-tower quarters
sites.el: Creek about 14 km long; property covers the first 4.5 km
sites.se: Wooden abras still ferry people across the creek where about 800 people settled in 1833 and dhows have traded ever since
sites.sa: ما زالت العبرات الخشبية تنقل الناس عبر الخور الذي استقر عند مصبه نحو 800 شخص عام 1833، ولا تزال المراكب الشراعية تتاجر فيه
sites.desc: Khor Dubai is a natural seawater inlet of the Arabian Gulf about 14 km long and 100 to 500 m wide, dividing Bur Dubai and Deira and ending at Ras Al Khor. Dubai is first recorded by the Venetian pearl merchant Gasparo Balbi in 1587, and in 1833 about 800 members of the Bani Yas settled at the creek mouth. The creek was dredged in 1961 to admit vessels drawing 2.1 m. The Tentative List property covers the first 4.5 km, including Shindagha, Bastakia with its wind-towers, the Deira souqs and Al Fahidi Fort.
sites.sig: A living traditional harbour where dhow trade and abra crossings continue at the core of a global city.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 5662
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2012). Khor Dubai (Dubai Creek), a traditional merchants' harbour, Tentative List ref. 5662. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5662

sites.s: Four-domed stone-and-mud mosque · oldest mosque in the UAE still in use
sites.el: 6.8 × 6.8 m, four domes on one pillar
sites.se: A small square mosque in Fujairah whose four domes rest on a single stone pillar, still used for prayer after about 500 years
sites.sa: مسجد مربع صغير في الفجيرة تستند قبابه الأربع إلى عمود حجري واحد، وما زالت الصلاة تقام فيه منذ نحو خمسة قرون
sites.desc: A small square mosque of stone and mud in Al Bidya, Fujairah, measuring 6.8 × 6.8 m, with four domes of unequal size supported by one central pillar. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from the foundation gives a construction window of 1450–1670 AD (95% probability) and 1480–1650 AD (68%). The walls have dentate carvings, light openings and lamp niches; the mihrab is 180 cm high and 90 cm wide. It is described as the oldest mosque in the UAE still in use, and watchtowers, house foundations and petroglyphs lie nearby.
sites.sig: A rare surviving pre-modern mosque of the east coast that is still in daily use.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 5665
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2012). Al Bidya Mosque, Tentative List ref. 5665. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5665

sites.n: Pearl trading town of Jazirat Al Hamra
sites.s: Abandoned coral-stone pearling town · houses, souq, mosques and fort
sites.el: 45 ha former island; about 500 houses in 1908
sites.te: The town the pearl divers left
sites.se: A whole town of coral-stone houses in Ras Al Khaimah, built on pearling and left almost untouched since its people moved out around 1970
sites.sa: بلدة كاملة من بيوت الحجر المرجاني في رأس الخيمة، قامت على الغوص على اللؤلؤ وبقيت على حالها تقريبًا منذ رحيل أهلها نحو عام 1970
sites.desc: A former 45 ha island in a lagoon on the southern coast of Ras Al Khaimah, thought to date from the 17th century as it is absent from Gasparo Balbi's 1580 list. It was first described in 1756, mapped by the British in 1820, and in 1908 J.G. Lorimer counted 500 houses in two quarters, the main town of the Za'ab tribe who lived mainly from pearl diving. Houses of coral stone and fossil beach rock, a souq, mosques and a fort survive, including the two-storey Bait Omran and the wind-tower house of Bait Abdul Karim. Its inhabitants left between 1968 and 1971.
sites.sig: One of the best-preserved traditional pearling towns of the Arabian Gulf coast.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 6464
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2020). The pearl trading town of Jazirat Al-Hamra, Tentative List ref. 6464. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6464

sites.s: Fort mound on Dibba Bay · Neolithic to 20th century, Qasimi governor's seat
sites.te: A fort built on thousands of years
sites.se: Under the fort of Dibba Al-Hisn lie layers from the Stone Age to the last century, with glass workshops, date presses and a fish factory
sites.sa: تحت حصن دبا الحصن طبقات تمتد من العصر الحجري الحديث إلى القرن الماضي، فيها ورش للزجاج ومدابس للتمر ومصنع للسمك المملح
sites.desc: The northern component of the Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, on Dibba Bay at the southern edge of the Musandam Peninsula. The fort mound has a stratigraphic sequence from the Neolithic to the 20th century, with three circular bastion foundations, glass-working workshops, twelve madabis for date processing, pearl-processing installations and a 19th-century salted fish factory. Portuguese forces reportedly seized the site in 1624 CE, a phase known from maps but not yet confirmed by excavation. The surviving fabric is mainly Qasimi, and the fort served as a governor's residence and court in the 19th and 20th centuries.
sites.sig: Part of a chain of east-coast forts tracing the shift from Hormuzi trade to Portuguese and then Al Qasimi control.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 7039
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2026). Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, Tentative List ref. 7039 (submitted 28/07/2026). https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/7039/

sites.s: East and West forts and walled old town · Portuguese, Arab and Qasimi phases
sites.se: On Khor Fakkan's bay, one fort was rebuilt three times, by the Portuguese, by Arab rulers and by the Qawasim
sites.sa: على خليج خورفكان أُعيد بناء حصن واحد ثلاث مرات: على يد البرتغاليين، ثم الحكام العرب، ثم القواسم
sites.desc: The central component of the Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, on a sheltered crescent bay of the Sea of Oman. The East Fort is a stone enclosure with three towers and an Arabic inscription recording the Qasimi takeover. The West Fort has three superimposed phases: a triangular plan interpreted as 17th-century Portuguese, a rectangular structure of the later 18th century and a square fort with a round tower of the 19th century. The old town has occupation layers and stone houses of the 15th to early 16th centuries and a surviving medieval town wall more than 155 m long; a Portuguese fort was built here in 1620 CE.
sites.sig: A layered harbour fortification recording three centuries of contest over the Sea of Oman coast.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 7039
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2026). Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, Tentative List ref. 7039 (submitted 28/07/2026). https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/7039/

sites.s: Portuguese rammed-earth fort at the Khor Kalba creek · later Qasimi fort
sites.el: Quadrangular fort with two round corner towers
sites.te: The Portuguese fort by the mangroves
sites.se: At the mouth of the mangrove creek of Kalba, the Portuguese built a rammed-earth fort in 1624, later abandoned, perhaps as the creek silted up
sites.sa: عند مصب خور كلباء بين أشجار القرم بنى البرتغاليون عام 1624 حصنًا من التراب المدكوك، هُجر لاحقًا، ربما حين امتلأ الخور بالطمي
sites.desc: The southern component of the Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, on a sandy plain at the mouth of the Khor Kalba tidal creek and mangrove lagoon. Under the Kingdom of Hormuz it was a fortified settlement governed by a Qasimi chief before Portuguese forces seized it in 1624 CE. The Portuguese built a rammed-earth fort on stone foundations, used as a navigation aid, trading station and supply depot; excavations show a quadrangular enclosure with two circular corner towers and a south entrance. It was probably abandoned in the 18th century, possibly as the creek silted, and a later fort to the north-east reflects Al Qasimi consolidation in the 18th and 19th centuries.
sites.sig: Archaeological evidence of the Portuguese supply network on the Sea of Oman coast and its Qasimi successor.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 7039
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2026). Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, Tentative List ref. 7039 (submitted 28/07/2026). https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/7039/

sites.s: First rock art site found in the Hajar Mountains · extinct wild asses and ibex
sites.p: 5th millennium BCE – 2nd millennium BCE and later
sites.se: Near Kalba, people carved wild asses that no longer exist, then ibex over them, thousands of years ago
sites.sa: قرب كلباء نقش الناس قبل آلاف السنين صور حمير برية لم تعد موجودة، ثم نقشوا فوقها صور الوعول
sites.desc: A rock art site near Kalba and the border with Oman, the first rock art site discovered in the Hajar Mountains and a component of The Rock Art of the Emirate of Sharjah on the UNESCO Tentative List (2023). The oldest phase, around the 5th millennium BCE, shows wild asses, probably the extinct Syrian wild ass (Equus hemionus hemippus). These are overlain by 4th-millennium BCE ibex or wild goats in the three-strokes style, and a third phase of the 3rd–2nd millennium BCE and later adds abstract designs and human figures. It also has naturalistic, dynamic animal figures not found elsewhere in the region.
sites.sig: A long, layered record of prehistoric art and of a wild ass now extinct.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 6642
disc: First Hajar rock art site found
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). The Rock Art of the Emirate of Sharjah, Tentative List ref. 6642. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6642

sites.s: Offshore salt-dome island · top UAE hawksbill nesting site and seabird colonies
sites.dr: Protected 2000; Ramsar site no. 2191 (2013); UNESCO Tentative List 2012
sites.se: Far out in the Arabian Gulf, this colourful salt-dome island is where more hawksbill turtles nest than anywhere else in the UAE
sites.sa: في عرض الخليج العربي تقع هذه الجزيرة الملحية الملوّنة التي تعشّش فيها سلاحف منقار الصقر أكثر من أي مكان آخر في الإمارات
sites.desc: An offshore island about 110 km from Sharjah formed by a mineral-rich salt dome, whose iron oxide and sulfur were mined in the past. Protected by Decree No. 25 of 2000, it was listed as Ramsar site no. 2191 on 2 December 2013 (4,964 ha, including 1,333 ha of land) and placed on the UNESCO Tentative List in 2012. It is the UAE's most important hawksbill turtle nesting site and supports nesting Socotra cormorants, red-billed tropicbirds, terns and more than 1% of the regional sooty gull breeding population. Ramsar records 40 coral and 76 reef fish species, and pottery about 3,500 years old has been found there.
sites.sig: A rare combination of salt-dome geology, turtle nesting beaches, seabird colonies and coral reefs.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 5661; Ramsar annotated summary (2191)

sites.s: Bronze Age copper mining and smelting valley in the Hajar ophiolite
sites.se: In Wadi Al Helo, Bronze Age people dug copper from hard rock and smelted it in furnaces set high up to catch the wind
sites.sa: في وادي الحلو استخرج أهل العصر البرونزي النحاس من صخر صلب، وصهروه في أفران أقاموها في الأعالي لتلتقط الريح
sites.desc: A valley of about 84 km² in the Hajar Mountains of Sharjah, listed on the UNESCO Tentative List in 2023 as testimony of Bronze Age copper production in south-east Arabia. Copper was mined in open workings in hard ophiolite and smelted in furnaces placed on high ground to use the wind, fuelled by acacia wood. Remains include slag heaps, workshops, a casting pit and a watchtower at the valley entrance. The dossier links it to Bronze Age centres such as Tell Abraq, Kalba and Umm an-Nar, and rock art in the valley includes T-shaped figures, boats and Syrian wild asses.
sites.sig: A key source landscape for the copper trade of ancient Magan.
sites.ex: UNESCO Tentative List 6641
disc: Linked to Tell Abraq and Umm an-Nar
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Wadi Al Helo: Testimony of Bronze Age Copper Production, Tentative List ref. 6641. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6641

sites.conf: The source gives no dates; t0/t1 are a broad estimate for the Bronze Age in south-east Arabia (c. 3200–1300 BC). Wadi Al Helo is also a Sharjah nature reserve

sites.s: Falaj-fed palm oasis of Al Ain · forts, mosques and watchtower
sites.dr: UNESCO World Heritage 2011 (component of Cultural Sites of Al Ain)
sites.se: In Al Jimi Oasis a 14 m tower guarded the spot where the falaj water came up for people to drink
sites.sa: في واحة الجيمي كان برج بارتفاع 14 مترًا يحرس الموضع الذي تظهر فيه مياه الفلج ليشرب منها الناس
sites.desc: One of the six oases of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain World Heritage property, covering about 80 ha in a sunken basin divided into 185 palm-garden plots irrigated by a falaj. More than a dozen historic earthen buildings, including mosques, fortified houses and watchtowers, show its importance from the 18th century onward. The largest is the fortified house of Ahmad bin Hilal Al Dhaheri, governor of Al Ain from 1896 to 1937. The 14 m Jimi watchtower guarded the shariaa, where the falaj water reached the surface.
sites.sig: A living oasis that shows how falaj irrigation and fortified houses sustained life in Al Ain.
sites.ex: DCT Abu Dhabi (2025); UNESCO 1343

sites.s: Rocky ridge with Al Naqfa Fort ruins · commands the approach to Al Ain Oasis
sites.dr: UNESCO World Heritage 2011 (component of Cultural Sites of Al Ain)
sites.se: From this rocky ridge a fort watched over the road into Al Ain Oasis for more than three thousand years
sites.sa: من هذا المرتفع الصخري راقب حصنٌ الطريق المؤدي إلى واحة العين، وتشهد كسر الفخار على ارتياده منذ أكثر من ثلاثة آلاف عام
sites.desc: A component of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain World Heritage property, where the ruins of Al Naqfa Fort stand on a rocky outcrop overlooking and commanding the approach to Al Ain Oasis. Surface pottery dates from the Iron Age (1300–300 BCE) through the Late Islamic period (1650–1950 CE). A modern cemetery and communal prayer ground nearby show its continuing importance.
sites.sig: A strategic lookout showing long use of the ridges that guard the Al Ain oases.
sites.ex: DCT Abu Dhabi (2025); UNESCO 1343
disc: Iron Age to Late Islamic pottery

sites.s: Early Bronze Age beehive tombs north of Jebel Hafit · Hafit period
sites.dr: UNESCO World Heritage 2011 (component of Cultural Sites of Al Ain)
sites.el: Tombs up to about 8 m high
sites.se: On the ridges north of Jebel Hafit, round stone tombs about 5,000 years old held a few people each
sites.sa: على التلال شمال جبل حفيت مدافن حجرية مستديرة عمرها نحو خمسة آلاف عام، ضمّ كل منها بضعة أشخاص
sites.desc: One of four Hafit tomb sites in the Jebel Hafit area included in the Cultural Sites of Al Ain World Heritage property, assigned to the Hafit period (c. 3200–2700 BCE). Hafit tombs are round single-chamber towers up to about 8 m high and 5–7 m across, with two or three concentric ring walls and an entrance, usually holding 3–4 individuals. Grave goods include imported ceramic vessels, copper objects, beads and occasional shell and flint artefacts; about 50 Mesopotamian vessels have been recovered from Hafit tombs, mostly at Jebel Hafit and Garn Bint Saud.
sites.sig: Early Bronze Age monuments that mark the first contacts of the Al Ain area with Mesopotamia.
sites.ex: DCT Abu Dhabi (2025); UNESCO 1343

sites.na: مقطع وادي البيح للعصرين البرمي والترياسي
sites.s: Carbonate section that recorded ocean acidification during the greatest mass extinction
sites.el: pH fall of up to 0.7 over about 10,000 years
sites.te: Where the ancient sea turned sour
sites.se: Rocks in Wadi Bih show that the sea became more acidic during the worst extinction in Earth's history, about 252 million years ago
sites.sa: تكشف صخور وادي البيح أن مياه البحر ازدادت حموضة في أثناء أسوأ انقراض جماعي عرفته الأرض قبل نحو 252 مليون سنة
sites.desc: Wadi Bih in the Musandam Mountains of Ras Al Khaimah exposes a shallow-marine carbonate succession laid down on a wide platform connected to the Neo-Tethys Ocean. Boron isotopes from this section stepped up from about 10.9‰ to 15.3‰ at about 252.04 Ma, then fell to about 8.2‰, which Clarkson et al. (2015) calculate as a pH drop of up to 0.7. The acidification event began near 251.88 Ma, lasted about 10,000 years and coincides with the second pulse of the Permo-Triassic mass extinction. The authors link it to the preferential loss of heavily calcified marine life.
sites.sig: Boron isotopes from this UAE section are key evidence that ocean acidification helped drive the Permo-Triassic mass extinction.
sites.ex: Clarkson et al. (2015), Science
refs: Clarkson, M.O., Kasemann, S.A., Wood, R.A., Lenton, T.M., Daines, S.J., Richoz, S., Ohnemueller, F., Meixner, A., Poulton, S.W. & Tipper, E.T. (2015). Ocean acidification and the Permo-Triassic mass extinction. Science 348(6231), 229–232. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa0193
Clarkson, M.O. et al. (2015). (Table S1) Boron, carbon and oxygen isotope data from Wadi Bih, United Arab Emirates. PANGAEA. https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.845819
sites.conf: Coordinates are the Wadi_Bih event in the PANGAEA dataset (25.842, 56.11158). Timeline spans the two dated events in the source (about 252.04 Ma and 251.88 Ma), not the whole section. Arabic name is a descriptive translation.

sites.na: مقطع وادي النقب عند الحد بين العصرين الترياسي والجوراسي
sites.s: Equatorial carbonate ramp that crossed the end-Triassic extinction
sites.dr: Ghalilah Formation to basal Musandam Limestone; boundary about 201.3 Ma
sites.te: A reef sea at the edge of an extinction
sites.se: In Wadi Naqab, layers of ancient sea floor run straight through the end-Triassic extinction, about 201 million years ago
sites.sa: في وادي النقب تمتد طبقات من قاع بحر قديم عبر الانقراض الذي ختم العصر الترياسي قبل نحو 201 مليون سنة
sites.desc: Wadi Naqab in Ras Al Khaimah is one of four logged sections of an equatorial mixed carbonate–siliciclastic ramp on the Musandam Peninsula. The Ghalilah Formation here includes a Sakhra Member oolite about 26 m thick and a Shuba Member about 50 m thick, followed by a 7 m cross-bedded ooid grainstone at the base of the Musandam Limestone. Hönig et al. (2017) place the Triassic–Jurassic boundary at the Shuba–Musandam transition using strontium isotope ages, carbon isotopes and fossils, and tentatively record a positive carbon-isotope shift of about 3.5–4‰. They found no clear evidence of a biocalcification crisis at the boundary.
sites.sig: A rare shallow tropical record of the end-Triassic mass extinction, used to test whether ocean acidification struck reef-building life.
sites.ex: Hönig et al. (2017), Gondwana Research
refs: Hönig, M.R., John, C.M. & Manning, C. (2017). Development of an equatorial carbonate platform across the Triassic–Jurassic boundary and links to global palaeoenvironmental changes (Musandam Peninsula, UAE/Oman). Gondwana Research, 100–117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gr.2016.11.007
sites.conf: Coordinates are the log base given by Hönig et al. (N 25°43′5.7″, E 56°05′14.1″). Timeline runs from the maximum brachiopod age at the top of the Asfal Member (about 208.3 Ma) to the boundary age used (about 201.3 Ma). Arabic name is a descriptive translation.

sites.s: Late Triassic shallow-sea limestones of the Ghalilah Formation
sites.dr: Ghalilah Formation (Asfal, Sumra, Sakhra and Shuba members)
sites.te: A tropical sea in the mountains
sites.se: The cliffs of Wadi Ghalilah were once a warm sea near the equator, full of shells and reefs
sites.sa: كانت منحدرات وادي غليلة يومًا بحرًا دافئًا قرب خط الاستواء يعجّ بالأصداف والشعاب
sites.desc: Wadi Ghalilah in northern Ras Al Khaimah is a logged section of the Ghalilah Formation, which records a shallow equatorial carbonate ramp on the Musandam Peninsula. The formation is divided into the Asfal, Sumra, Sakhra and Shuba members; the Asfal Member was deposited after about 232 Ma and the Shuba Member is about 60 m thick at this section. Al-Suwaidi et al. (2016) describe the Ghalilah Formation as a complete, continuous shallow-water carbonate sequence from the Upper Triassic into the Lower Jurassic, with a negative carbon-isotope excursion reaching about –2.8‰ just below the boundary. Their data point to aragonite supersaturation, rather than acidification, at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary.
sites.sig: A continuous equatorial shallow-water record of the Late Triassic and the end-Triassic extinction, where many higher-latitude sections have gaps.
sites.ex: Hönig et al. (2017); Al-Suwaidi et al. (2016)
disc: Four members: Asfal, Sumra, Sakhra, Shuba
refs: Hönig, M.R., John, C.M. & Manning, C. (2017). Development of an equatorial carbonate platform across the Triassic–Jurassic boundary and links to global palaeoenvironmental changes (Musandam Peninsula, UAE/Oman). Gondwana Research, 100–117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gr.2016.11.007

Al-Suwaidi, A.H., Steuber, T. & Suarez, M.B. (2016). The Triassic–Jurassic boundary event from an equatorial carbonate platform (Ghalilah Formation, United Arab Emirates). Journal of the Geological Society. https://doi.org/10.1144/jgs2015-102
sites.conf: Coordinates are the Wadi Ghalilah log base given by Hönig et al. (N 25°58′23.1″, E 56°05′40.5″). Al-Suwaidi et al. describe the formation as a whole; the source does not say their samples came from this exact section. Timeline runs from about 232 Ma (after which the Asfal Member was deposited) to the boundary age used (about 201.3 Ma).

sites.s: Pale granite dykes cutting the Semail ophiolite mantle on the Fujairah coast
sites.dr: Leucogranite and tonalite dykes, about 92.4–91.0 Ma
sites.te: White granite in the dark mantle
sites.se: At Ras Dadnah, white granite veins slice through dark rocks that once lay deep beneath the ocean floor
sites.sa: في رأس ضدنا تشقّ عروق من الجرانيت الأبيض صخورًا داكنة كانت يومًا في أعماق ما تحت قاع المحيط
sites.desc: Ras Dadnah on the Fujairah coast exposes felsic dykes and sills that intrude mantle rocks of the Semail ophiolite. Rioux et al. (2021) dated a tourmaline–garnet leucogranite here at 92.361 ± 0.026 Ma, a biotite tonalite from a composite sill at 91.292 ± 0.061 Ma and a tonalite west of Ras Dadnah at 90.998 ± 0.052 Ma. These ages are younger than the main ophiolite crust and are used to study melting during subduction initiation. In a 2024 geoheritage evaluation, the Ras Dadnah leucogranite outcrop ranked highest of the Fujairah sites for scientific value.
sites.sig: A rare, easily reached exposure of granite formed inside an ophiolite mantle, dated to within tens of thousands of years.
sites.ex: Rioux et al. (2021); Sayama et al. (2024)
refs: Rioux, M., Garber, J.M., Searle, M., Kelemen, P., Miyashita, S., Adachi, Y. & Bowring, S. (2021). High-precision U-Pb zircon dating of late magmatism in the Samail ophiolite: A record of subduction initiation. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 126, e2020JB020758. https://doi.org/10.1029/2020JB020758

Sayama, K., Parker, A.G., Parton, A. & Viles, H. (2024). Reflecting Experiences of Regional Academic, Tourism, and Education Specialists in Geoheritage Evaluation for Fujairah, UAE and Southeast Arabia. Geoheritage 16, 90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12371-024-00995-1

sites.s: Mingled dark and pale magmas of the Semail ophiolite's late crust
sites.se: Near Fujairah, dark and light rocks swirl together like oil and vinegar, frozen from two magmas that met underground
sites.sa: قرب الفجيرة تتداخل صخور داكنة وأخرى فاتحة كالزيت والخل، تجمّدت من صهارتين التقتا في باطن الأرض
sites.desc: West of Fujairah city the ophiolite crust contains intrusions of the Fujairah facies, where dark gabbro and pale tonalite are mingled in so-called vinaigrette textures. Goodenough et al. (2010) dated the felsic part of one such intrusion at 95.26 ± 0.31 Ma. They showed that this later magmatic sequence formed over about 1.2 million years, between about 96.40 and 95.26 Ma, and that obduction began around 94.5 Ma. Rioux et al. (2021) also dated Fujairah gabbro and tonalites from the Aswad block.
sites.sig: Key evidence that the Oman–UAE ophiolite crust was built in more than one magmatic phase just before it was thrust onto Arabia.
sites.ex: Goodenough et al. (2010)
disc: Late magmatism lasted about 1.2 million years
refs: Goodenough, K.M., Styles, M.T., Schofield, D., Thomas, R.J., Crowley, Q.C., Lilly, R.M., McKervey, J., Stephenson, D. & Carney, J.N. (2010). Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 126, e2020JB020758. https://doi.org/10.1029/2020JB020758

Timeline is the span of the later magmatic sequence given in the source.

sites.s: Largest exposure of the ophiolite's metamorphic sole in the UAE
sites.te: Rocks baked under a sliding ocean floor
sites.ta: صخور طُهيت تحت قاع محيط زاحف
sites.se: Around Masafi lie rocks that were squeezed and heated as a slab of ocean floor slid over the edge of Arabia
sites.sa: حول مسافي تنتشر صخور انضغطت وسخنت حين زحفت كتلة من قاع المحيط فوق حافة الجزيرة العربية
sites.desc: The Masafi–Ghub area is the largest exposure of metamorphic rocks beneath the Semail ophiolite in the UAE, covering about 100 km². It consists of greenschist- to locally amphibolite-facies quartz–chlorite schists, metacherts and minor meta-carbonate and meta-volcanic rocks of the Masafi–Ismah Group. A quartz schist sample gave a rutile age of 94.1 ± 2.6 Ma, and garnet–diopside amphibolites in the Masafi area record about 800 ± 100 °C and 1.1 ± 0.2 GPa. Carbonatites in the underlying Jebel Hakimah Group have a zircon age of 103 ± 1 Ma.
sites.sig: The window shows the hot metamorphic sole formed as the ophiolite began to move, and separates the Khor Fakkan and Aswad ophiolite blocks.
sites.ex: Roberts et al. (2016); Goodenough et al. (2010)
refs: Roberts, N.M.W., Thomas, R.J. & Jacobs, J. (2016). Geochronological constraints on the metamorphic sole of the Semail ophiolite in the United Arab Emirates. Geoscience Frontiers 7, 609–619. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gsf.2015.12.003

Goodenough, K.M., Styles, M.T., Schofield, D., Thomas, R.J., Crowley, Q.C., Lilly, R.M., McKervey, J., Stephenson, D. & Carney, J.N. (2010). Architecture of the Oman–UAE ophiolite: evidence for a multi-phase magmatic history. Arabian Journal of Geosciences 3(4), 439–458. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12517-010-0177-3
sites.conf: No published outcrop coordinate was found; coordinates are those of Masafi town (25°18′48″N, 56°9′46″E, gazetteer/Wikipedia), which the Fujairah–Ras Al Khaimah border runs through. The pressure–temperature estimate is Gnos (1998) as cited by Roberts et al. Timeline runs from the 103 Ma carbonatites to the 94.1 Ma rutile age.

sites.n: Wadi Ham Fault Zone at Al Bithnah
sites.na: نطاق صدع وادي حام عند البثنة
sites.s: Major fault corridor between two blocks of the Semail ophiolite
sites.dr: NW–SE fault zone in the Semail ophiolite
sites.el: Separates the Khor Fakkan and Aswad blocks
sites.te: The valley that splits the mountains
sites.se: Wadi Ham follows a great break in the rocks that splits the mountains into two giant blocks of old ocean floor
sites.sa: يسير وادي حام على امتداد كسر عظيم في الصخور يقسم الجبال إلى كتلتين هائلتين من قاع محيط قديم
sites.desc: Wadi Ham runs from Masafi to Fujairah city and the Gulf of Oman, with the village of Al Bithnah on its route. The British Geological Survey mapped a north-west to south-east fault zone along it that bounds the southern side of the Khor Fakkan ophiolite block and separates it from the Aswad block. The Aswad block is about 70 km north–south and holds the most extensive network of younger gabbros in the UAE ophiolite. Layered gabbros near Bithnah are mostly horizontal to gently inclined.
sites.sig: The fault zone is one of the main structural boundaries that divide the UAE part of the Semail ophiolite into separate blocks, and has long served as a mountain pass.
sites.ex: Goodenough et al. (2010); Heikal (1999)
disc: Separates Khor Fakkan and Aswad blocks
Ancient route through the Hajar Mountains

sites.s: Neolithic ritual platform of dugong bones in the Umm Al Quwain lagoon
sites.dr: Settlement c. 4748–3814 BC; dugong mound 3522–3226 BC (2σ)
sites.el: More than 40 dugongs in a 10 m² mound
sites.te: The island of the sea-cow shrine
sites.se: On a small island, Stone Age fishers carefully stacked the skulls and bones of more than 40 dugongs into a sacred platform
sites.sa: على جزيرة صغيرة رتّب صيادو العصر الحجري جماجم أكثر من 40 أطومًا وعظامها في منصة مقدسة
sites.desc: Akab is a small island in Khor al-Beidah, the lagoon of Umm Al Quwain, first found in 1989 and excavated again in 2006–2008. Its Late Neolithic settlement is dated by radiocarbon to between about 4748 and 3814 BC. An ovoid mound of about 10 m² and 0.30–0.40 m high holds the remains of more than 40 dugongs, with mandibles forming a base and skulls aligned in rows, together with several hundred objects such as shell and soft-stone beads; it is dated to 3522–3226 BC. Fish bones from the site belong to 56 bony-fish species in 42 genera and 22 families.
sites.sig: Described by its excavators as the oldest known ritual site associated with the dugong.
sites.ex: Méry et al. (2009); Lidour et al. (2019)
refs: Méry, S., Charpentier, V., Auxiette, G. & Pelle, E. (2009). A dugong bone mound: the Neolithic ritual site on Akab in Umm al-Quwain, United Arab Emirates. Lidour, K., Béarez, P., Charpentier, V. & Méry, S. (2019). The Prehistoric Fisheries of Akab Island (United Arab Emirates): New Insights into Coastal Subsistence during Neolithic in Eastern Arabia. The Journal of Island and Coastal Archaeology. https://doi.org/10.1080/15564894.2018.1531330
sites.conf: Coordinates are from Lidour et al. (2019), whose text lost its degree symbols; read as 25°34′09.94″N, 55°34′31.67″E, which agrees within about 3 km with the gazetteer point for Akab Island. Timeline years are converted from the calibrated BC dates. Wikipedia gives the Arabic name as جزيرة الأكعاب; عكاب is the common local spelling.

sites.n: Umm Al Quwain spit and lagoon system
sites.na: لسان أم القيوين الرملي ونظامه الساحلي
sites.s: Holocene sand spit and barrier lagoon shaped by sea-level change
sites.dr: Sea level about 2 m higher around 5,500 BP
sites.te: A town on a ribbon of sand

sites.desc: The city of Umm Al Quwain is built on a coastal dune system along the main spit that encloses Khor al-Beidah, a lagoon about 20 km long, 8 km wide and about 127 km² in area. About 8 km² was reclaimed between 1965 and 1984, and grey mangrove cover has expanded since 1984 as dredging improved tidal flushing.

sites.s: Old port and first air station of the lower Gulf · UNESCO Tentative List 2014

sites.desc: The old part of Sharjah, including its old port and old airport, was placed on the UNESCO Tentative List in 2014 as the gate to the Trucial States. The port lies in a protected sea inlet (Al Khor), and the 11th-century geographer Al Idrisi referred to a port here. Under the Qawasim, Sharjah was the most important port of the lower Arabian Gulf into the first half of the 19th century; it was devastated in 1820 but recovered, and in 1932 it became an air station linking the West with India, now the Al Mahatta Museum. The historic town keeps a fort, mosques, markets, narrow streets, courtyard houses, wind towers and remains of its old walls.

sites.desc: A double-storey traditional fortification of rock, coral and mudbrick in central Ajman, thought to date to the late 18th century. It was the seat of the Al Nuaimi rulers: it was destroyed during the British punitive expedition of 1819, changed hands several times in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and in 1967 became the headquarters of Ajman Police until 1978. After restoration in the early 1980s it became the Ajman Museum, established on 20 May 1991, whose displays include an excavated cemetery from Al Muwaihat with pottery and funerary jewellery dating back as far as 3000 BC. The fort is the centrepiece of the Dhs 25 million Ajman Heritage District, opened in October 2020.
